wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e111.summary: Rubric introducing the single question on Distinction 37 of Book I.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e122.summary: States the question: whether being everywhere and in all things by essence, presence and power belongs properly to God alone.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e131.summary: First objection, against the claim that ubiquity belongs to God at all: what belongs to something by essence belongs to it necessarily and always, but being in all things does not belong to God necessarily and always, because before creation there were no things for God to be in.
claims: What belongs to something per essentiam belongs to it necessarily and always.
Before creation God was not in any creatures.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e144.summary: Second objection: if God were in all things he would be in place. By analogy, whatever is informed by a quality can be altered in quality, so whatever is in place can be moved locally. God cannot be moved locally, so he is not in place and therefore not in all things.
claims: What is in place is necessarily locally mobile.
God is in no way locally mobile.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e169.summary: Third objection, against ubiquity being proper to God: a universal is everywhere by essence and therefore also by power, in the way it has power, so ubiquity is not unique to God.
claims: A universal is everywhere by essence.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e176.summary: The sed contra: appeal to the Master (Peter Lombard) in the text of the distinction.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e181.summary: States that the conclusion is settled among theologians: it is proper to God alone to be in all existing things, and in possible things if they were posited, by essence, presence and power. The real inquiry concerns the reasons for this.
claims: It is proper to God alone to be in all existing things, and in possible things if posited, by essence, presence and power.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e190.summary: Identifies the specific difficulty: whether it follows from God being in all things by power, as their immediate cause, that he is everywhere by essence.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e201.summary: Reports the view of some (in substance Aquinas's account) that God is in all things by power insofar as all are subject to his power, by presence insofar as all lie open to his sight, and by essence insofar as he is present to all as the cause of their being. They prove the last point from Aristotle's principle (Physics VII) that agent and patient, mover and moved, must be together, since God is the agent cause of everything.
claims: God is in all things by power, presence and essence in three distinct ways (reported view).
An agent must be conjoined with what it immediately acts on (reported premise).
Because God immediately causes all things, he is in all things by essence (reported conclusion).

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e221.summary: Rejects as false in general the principle that mover and moved, agent and patient, must be locally together, using a thought experiment about sunlight. When a sunbeam through a window ends on an opaque body, the light there must be caused immediately by the sun. It cannot be caused only by nearby light, because an active principle equally close to equally disposed patients would produce equal effects in both, yet a patient shaded from the sun by an opaque body is plainly not illuminated equally. So the sun acts immediately at a distance.
claims: Agent and patient need not be locally together.
An active principle equally close to equally disposed patients, with no impediment, produces equal effects.
The sun immediately causes light in a distant body.
Nearby light alone cannot explain the observed difference in illumination.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e268.summary: Rebuts the reply that the nearby light acts only in the power of the sun, which causes and conserves it. Ockham asks what 'in the sun's power' means. (1) That the nearby light depends on the sun for conservation: a conserved agent still acts equally on equally close patients, as with moonlight or fire conserved by another. (2) That the sun sends it some power: the same argument applies to that natural power. (3) That the sun co-acts: this grants that the sun acts immediately at a distance. He also rejects saying the sun acts at a distance only mediately: if it acted only mediately, then with the sun removed and its light divinely conserved the same effect would follow, which is false.
claims: Dependence on a conserver does not change how a natural agent acts on equally disposed, equally close patients.
Any power the sun sends to nearby light would itself act uniformly.
If the sun co-acts with nearby light, it acts immediately at a distance.
If an agent acts only mediately, the effect follows when that agent is removed and its intermediary is conserved.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e351.summary: Uses the same reasoning to close off the reply that the opaque body between the sun and the shaded patient is an impediment. A medium impedes only when it lies between the patient and the immediate agent. If the sun were not an immediate agent, the body between it and the patient would not impede anything, unless it stood between the patient and the nearby light, which the opponents make the sole immediate agent.
claims: A medium impedes an action only if it lies between the patient and the immediate agent.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e369.summary: Gives Ockham's own position: God is not in all things by essence precisely because he causes them. 'This acts on that, therefore it is in or present to it' is not a formal consequence. He then sets out a three-part plan: distinguish the saints' modes of God's being in things; show that God is in things by each mode; ask whether any mode can belong to another being.
claims: 'X acts on Y, therefore X is in Y' is not a formal consequence.
God's being in all things by essence is not grounded precisely in his causing them.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e389.summary: First article: following the saints and the Master, God is in all things generally and in some things specially. The general modes are power, presence and essence. Being in something by power simply means having it subject to one's power. In this sense even a corporeal thing can be 'in' something it is locally distant from, as the sun is in lower things or a king in his kingdom, though philosophers rarely speak this way.
claims: God is in all things generally and in some things specially.
To be in something by power is to have it subject to one's power.
Presence by power is compatible with local distance.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e413.summary: Continues the analysis of the modes. Presence has two senses. (a) Cognitive presence: being sufficiently present to a knower to be known, which allows local distance and is the sense in which all things are present to God. (b) Spatial presence: both exist and neither is locally distant from the other, so that place and placed are mutually present, even if philosophers say only that the placed is in place. Ockham notes that although 'esse in' is general in its signification, usage favors some applications. Being in something by essence means being in it with neither the thing nor any intrinsic part of it distant, wherever it or its parts are, as form is in matter. He also distinguishes the special modes: by informing grace, by special acceptation, and most specially in Christ by union.
claims: Presence can mean being sufficiently present to a knower, which is compatible with local distance.
Presence can also mean that neither of two existing things is locally distant from the other.
To be in something by essence is to be wherever it or any of its parts is, without distance.
God is specially in some things by grace (informing or by acceptation) and in Christ by union.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e476.summary: Second article: God is in all things by each mode. By power, because he is the cause of all things and has them in his power. By cognitive presence, because he knows all things perfectly and distinctly, as shown earlier. By spatial presence, by elimination: a real thing is not nowhere, and God cannot be present to some things and not others. If he could be present to another thing he could change place, which is impossible for him, and being limited to one thing rather than another is unfitting and diminishes his perfection. By essence, because God cannot be distant from every thing, so he is in some thing by essence and no more in one than another, hence in all. The special modes by grace and by union are referred to earlier and later discussions.
claims: God is in all things by power because he is the cause of all things.
All things are present to God's cognition.
No really existing thing is nowhere and distant from everything.
God cannot be present to some things and not others without being able to change place or being limited.
God is in every thing by essence.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e538.summary: Third article: by divine power some being other than God could, in some posited case, be in all other created things by power, presence and essence. What is proper to God alone is that the very existence of anything entails that he is in it: 'a exists, therefore God is in a by power, etc.' is valid, but not for any other being. This is how the saints mean it.
claims: By divine power a creature could be in all other created things by power, presence and essence.
It is proper to God alone that the existence of any thing entails his being in it.
The consequence 'a exists, therefore God is in a' holds for God and no other being.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e556.summary: Answers the question: being everywhere and in all other things in these modes is proper to God alone in the second sense just set out, that his presence follows from the mere existence of things. Being in all other creatures in these modes in the first sense, as a matter of fact, could belong to a creature by divine power.
claims: Ubiquity in the sense of necessary consequence from the existence of things is proper to God alone.
A creature could by divine power be in all other creatures in fact.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e574.summary: Answers the argument for the first opinion: Aristotle's intent in Metaphysics VII, concerning movers that produce effects of the same kind in the end-point and the medium, is that some mover is together with the moved. Beyond it there is another agent and mover that is not together with the moved and yet moves it immediately. Fuller treatment of the authority is deferred to Book II.
claims: Aristotle's principle allows an immediate mover that is not together with what it moves.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e600.summary: Answers the first principal argument by distinguishing senses of 'per essentiam'. (1) As equivalent to 'per se' in the sense of Posterior Analytics I: God is not everywhere by essence in this sense. (2) As meaning that God's essence is what the predicate immediately belongs to: God is everywhere by his essence in this sense, but not necessarily. (3) In the sense explained above, of non-distance.
claims: 'Per essentiam' can mean per se, being the immediate bearer of a predicate, or non-distant presence.
God is not everywhere per essentiam in the sense of per se.
God is everywhere by his essence as immediate bearer of the predicate, but not necessarily.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e620.summary: Answers the second principal argument: the relation between being informed by a quality and having the quality differs from the relation between being in place and what is in place, so the analogy fails and the argument does not conclude.
claims: The analogy between quality-informing and being in place does not hold.

wo8uy7-d1e1663-d1e625.summary: Answers the third principal argument: a universal is not everywhere, and Aristotle does not mean that. He means that 'being here' is predicated of the universal wherever it is predicated of something contained under it, not for the universal itself but for that singular, since the common term 'man' supposits for its contents. In the same way 'man is singular' is true without the common nature being singular.
claims: A universal is not everywhere.
Predicates verified of a singular are verified of the common term, but for the singular, not for the common term itself.
'Man is singular' is true, yet the common term 'man' is not singular.

wo8uy7-d1e1663.summary: The single question on Book I, Distinction 37 asks whether being everywhere and in all things by essence, presence and power is proper to God alone. Ockham accepts the theological consensus but rejects the standard (in substance Aquinas's) grounding of God's essential presence in his immediate causality, which relies on the principle that mover and moved must be together. Through an extended argument about sunlight on a shaded body he argues that natural agents such as the sun act immediately at a distance, so 'X acts on Y, therefore X is in Y' is not a formal consequence. He then distinguishes the modes of being in: by power (having in one's power), by presence (cognitive presence, or spatial non-distance), and by essence (non-distance of the thing and its parts, like form in matter), along with God's special presence by grace and by union. He argues that God is in all things by each mode, using an elimination argument: God cannot be nowhere or limited to some things. He concludes that what is uniquely divine is not de facto ubiquity, which God could grant to a creature, but the fact that the existence of any thing entails God's presence in it. Replies to the principal arguments distinguish senses of 'per essentiam' and reject the analogy between place and quality. A final reply denies that universals are everywhere: a predicate verified of a singular is verified of the common term only for that singular, by personal supposition.
claims: Agents can act immediately at a distance, so causality does not by itself entail presence.
God is in all things by power, presence and essence, each analyzed precisely.
What is proper to God alone is that the existence of any thing entails his presence in it.
A creature could by divine power be in fact present in all other creatures.
